title: Evidence Essentials 🔎
description: Understand the nature of digital evidence, its volatility, and the chain of custody that protects it.

slides.title: What Makes Digital Evidence Special? 💾
slides.content:
# Characteristics of Digital Evidence

Digital data is:
- **Latent**: Not visible to the naked eye – you need tools to extract it.
- **Fragile**: Easily altered or destroyed (a single click can wipe logs).
- **Voluminous**: Terabytes of data may hide a few relevant bytes.
- **Persistent**: Unlike human memory, deleted files often leave traces.

quizData.question: Digital evidence is usually visible without special tools.
quizData.explanation: Digital evidence is latent; it requires forensic tools and techniques to reveal its presence and meaning.

slides.title: Order of Volatility ⚡
slides.content:
When collecting evidence, capture the most volatile data first, because it disappears quickly. The general order:

1. **Registers / CPU cache** (nanoseconds)
2. **RAM** (lost when powered off)
3. **Network connections / running processes** (seconds to minutes)
4. **Disk storage** (persists but can be overwritten)
5. **Backups / archives** (most stable)

Following this order preserves crucial transient data.

quizData.question: According to the order of volatility, which should be collected first?
quizData.explanation: RAM and running processes are extremely volatile and vanish when a machine is shut down, so they must be captured first.

slides.title: Chain of Custody Deep Dive 🔗
slides.content:
A robust chain of custody form should include:
- **Item description**: Make, model, serial number.
- **Collection info**: Date, time, location, collector's name.
- **Every transfer**: Who received it, when, purpose.
- **Storage details**: Locked cabinet number, temperature, access controls.

> "If you didn't write it down, it didn't happen."

slides.title: Example: Timestamped Notes
slides.content: Forensic examiners often use scripts or logging tools to automatically record actions. A simple example:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Save command history with timestamps
echo "$(date): Starting disk image acquisition" >> case_notes.txt
sha256sum /dev/sdb >> case_notes.txt

quizData.question: Chain of custody only needs to record who initially collected the evidence.
quizData.explanation: It must track every person and action from collection to court, creating a complete audit trail.

slides.title: Hashing: The Integrity Seal 🔐
slides.content:
Before and after any operation, compute a hash (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) of the evidence. Matching hashes prove nothing changed.

- **Acquisition hash**: Taken right after imaging.
- **Verification hash**: Taken after analysis to confirm no accidental alteration.

If they don't match, your evidence is compromised.

slides.title: ⚠️ Never Work on the Original
slides.content: Always create a forensic image (bit-by-bit copy) and analyze that. Use write-blockers to prevent any changes to the original media.

quizData.question: What is the main reason to use a write-blocker when acquiring evidence?

options.text: To speed up the imaging process
To prevent any writes to the original evidence drive

quizData.explanation: A write-blocker ensures the source drive is read-only, preserving the integrity of the original evidence.
